content: 1. HIV infection is significantly influenced by the presence of other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), such as herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). Studies have demonstrated that HSV-2 plays a critical role in increasing the incidence of HIV, as it facilitates viral shedding and transmission. 2. Genital tract infections, including gonorrhea and chlamydia, have been shown to enhance HIV-1 shedding in the genital tract. This relationship has been systematically reviewed and analyzed, highlighting the importance of managing these infections to reduce HIV transmission. 3. Classical sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) such as syphilis, gonorrhea, and chancroid have historically driven the spread of HIV-1. These infections create mucosal disruptions and inflammatory responses that increase susceptibility to HIV acquisition. 4. The global strategy for the prevention and control of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) from 2006 to 2015 has been implemented to address the rising burden of STIs worldwide. Progress reports emphasize the need for continued efforts in surveillance, treatment, and prevention. 5. Antimicrobial resistance in gonococcal infections poses a significant public health challenge. Resistance to commonly used antibiotics, including quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, has been reported globally, necessitating updated treatment guidelines and strategies. 6. The development of vaccines for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is critical for global prevention efforts. Vaccines targeting pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis could significantly reduce the burden of these infections. 7. Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is the second most common bacterial STI worldwide, with an estimated 78 million new cases annually. The highest prevalence is observed in the WHO Western Pacific and African regions. 8. Co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis is detected in 10–40% of individuals with gonorrhea, underscoring the need for comprehensive diagnostic and treatment approaches. 9. In men, uncomplicated gonococcal infection typically presents as urethritis, characterized by urethral discharge and dysuria. The discharge may vary from scanty and mucoid to copious and purulent. 10. In women, gonorrhea is often asymptomatic, with less than half of infected individuals reporting non-specific symptoms such as abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, lower abdominal discomfort, or dyspareunia. Clinical signs include mucopurulent cervicitis with vaginal discharge and cervical friability. 11. Rectal infections in both men and women are largely asymptomatic but may occasionally cause rectal pain or discharge. Pharyngeal infections are also typically asymptomatic, though mild sore throat or pharyngitis may occur. 12. Untreated gonococcal infections can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women, which may result in infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. In men, complications include epididymitis, urethral stricture, and infertility. 13. Neonates born to mothers with gonococcal infection are at risk of neonatal conjunctivitis, presenting as purulent ocular discharge and swollen eyelids. If untreated, this condition can lead to scarring and blindness. 14. Laboratory diagnosis of Neisseria gonorrhoeae can be achieved through culture, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), and, in some cases, Gram stain. NAATs are highly sensitive and specific but do not provide antimicrobial susceptibility information, necessitating parallel culture testing. 15. Gram-stained smears are useful for presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men with urethritis but are less reliable for cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal infections. In low-resource settings, Gram stains may serve as a cost-effective alternative to NAATs for symptomatic men. 16. The increasing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) of Neisseria gonorrhoeae has necessitated updates to treatment guidelines. Resistance to quinolones and decreased susceptibility to third-generation cephalosporins have been reported, raising concerns about untreatable infections. 17. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of gonococcal infections aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for managing these infections and to support countries in updating their national treatment protocols. 18. The guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels, as well as policymakers and program managers involved in STI management. They emphasize the importance of addressing local AMR patterns and resource availability. 19. The guideline development process involved systematic reviews of evidence, prioritization of clinical questions, and the use of the GRADE approach to assess the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. 20. Recommendations were developed through consensus among international STI experts, considering the benefits and risks of interventions, patient values, resource use, and feasibility of implementation. 21. Strong recommendations are presented with the wording The WHO STI guideline recommends, while conditional recommendations use The WHO STI guideline suggests. The implications of these recommendations for patients, clinicians, and policymakers are clearly outlined. 22. Management of conflicts of interest was a priority throughout the guideline development process. Declarations of interest were obtained from all members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) to ensure transparency and minimize bias.
